query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) will reveal that high-temperature oxidation induces significant elemental redistribution within the nanoprecipitates of the additive‐manufactured dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, particularly evidenced by enrichment or depletion of key oxidation‐active elements (e.g., Al, Ti, Cr) at precipitate interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy produced via additive manufacturing, exhibiting nanoscale precipitates in a relatively homogeneous matrix.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA samples to controlled high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 850–1050 °C for a defined duration) and then analyze the oxidized microstructure using APT.
generation.conditions: Ex situ oxidation experiments performed under conditions that simulate high-temperature service environments (such as those in gas turbines or power plants), followed by atom probe analysis at near-atomic resolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitates acting as sites for elemental segregation and redistribution during oxidation.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature exposure drives diffusion processes that cause selective migration of oxidation‐active elements (like Al and Cr) within the nanoprecipitates, altering local compositions that APT can resolve in three dimensions.
generation.predicted_outcome: APT will detect measurable compositional gradients and phase separations within and around nanoprecipitates in the oxidized samples, confirming that oxidation triggers nanoscale elemental redistribution contributing to the alloy’s oxidation behavior.
generation.baseline: In the unoxidized (or conventionally processed cast/wrought) HEA samples, the nanoprecipitates exhibit a uniform elemental distribution that does not show the oxidation-induced gradients observed post-treatment.
generation.boundary: The extent and nature of the elemental redistribution may depend on the oxidation temperature, time, and potential external stresses; furthermore, capturing dynamic redistribution in real time remains uncertain—current evidence is based on ex situ snapshot analyses.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about the quantitative magnitude and uniformity of the elemental shifts within nanoprecipitates across different oxidation conditions, as well as potential artifacts introduced during specimen preparation for APT.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the additive‐manufactured HEA specimens. Subject one set to high-temperature oxidation (850–1050 °C for a specified duration) while keeping a control set unoxidized. Use APT to perform 3D compositional mapping on nanoprecipitates from both sets. Compare the elemental distributions to identify whether oxidation exposure yields statistically significant compositional gradients.
measurements: 3D elemental maps of nanoprecipitates using APT
Quantitative analysis of elemental concentration profiles within and around nanoprecipitates
Statistical comparison of oxidized vs. unoxidized samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT results show no significant difference in elemental distribution or gradients within nanoprecipitates between oxidized and unoxidized samples, the hypothesis that oxidation induces measurable elemental redistribution at the nanoscale is falsified.

[ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. decision.trend: Early studies on oxidation in high‐entropy alloys primarily adjusted the microstructure or applied protective coatings to improve oxidation resistance. For instance, one paper used stationary friction processing to achieve ultrafine grains in an AlCoCrFeNi system, which promoted the formation of protective oxides and decelerated oxidation kinetics. Another study improved oxidation resistance in a HfNbTaTiZr alloy by applying silicide coatings via pack cementation. While these approaches improved bulk oxidation performance, they did not probe the underlying nanoscale mechanisms, particularly the subtle elemental redistributions occurring in nanoprecipitates during oxidation.
decision.unsolved: The detailed mechanistic evolution and atomic-scale elemental redistribution within nanoprecipitates during high‐temperature oxidation remains largely unresolved. Existing measurement methods and microstructural characterizations do not offer the near-atomic resolution necessary to delineate the transformation and migration of individual elements within the nanoscale precipitates.
decision.lever: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) applied to in situ or ex situ oxidized samples
decision.why: APT provides near-atomic three-dimensional compositional mapping, which directly addresses the need for resolving subtle compositional changes in nanoprecipitates during oxidation. This method follows naturally from the trend—moving from macroscopic adjustments of oxidation resistance to probing the atomic-scale redistribution mechanisms—and is precisely aligned with the research question’s cues and constraints.
